mentions.quote: The *ācārya* is the lord of the world of Brahma
mentions.role: cosmic realm associated with the ācārya's spiritual authority

entities.description: The supreme divine being whose cosmic realm is presided over by the ācārya (teacher) in the cosmological hierarchy of worlds.
entities.justification: Brahma is named as the deity whose world (realm) the ācārya lords over, establishing a divine cosmological mapping in the text.

mentions.quote: the father is the lord in the world of Prajapati
mentions.role: cosmic realm associated with the father's authority

entities.description: The lord of creatures whose cosmic realm is presided over by the father in the cosmological hierarchy of social roles.
entities.justification: Prajapati is explicitly named in the mapping of human roles to divine worlds, linking paternal authority to his realm.

mentions.quote: the guest is the lord of the world of Indra
mentions.role: cosmic realm associated with the guest's honour

entities.description: The king of the gods whose cosmic realm is symbolically presided over by the honoured guest in the social-cosmic mapping.
entities.justification: Indra is named as the deity whose world the guest lords over, making him a touchstone for guest-honour ethics.

mentions.quote: The daughters-in-law are lords in the world of the Apsaras

entities.description: Celestial nymphs of the heavenly realm whose world is linked to daughters-in-law in the cosmological role-mapping.
entities.justification: The Apsaras are named as the divine inhabitants of the world governed by daughters-in-law in the social-cosmic hierarchy.

mentions.quote: the kinsmen, of the Vishve-devas

entities.description: The 'All-Gods,' a collective group of deities whose world is linked to kinsmen in the social-cosmic hierarchy.
entities.justification: Vishve-devas are named as the collective deity group whose realm is presided over by kinsmen, continuing the cosmological mapping.

mentions.quote: wanders for a hundred years in the hell called Tamisra
mentions.role: place of punishment for threatening a Brahmana

entities.description: A named hell realm ('Darkness') to which a twice-born who threatens to kill a Brahmana is condemned for a hundred years.
entities.justification: Tamisra is explicitly named as the hell a would-be Brahmana-killer wanders in, grounding it as a concrete punitive place.

mentions.quote: the rule of good conduct, which is the root of Dharma, as declared in *Śruti* and *Smṛti*
mentions.role: scriptural authority for the rule of good conduct

entities.description: The revealed scriptural corpus ('that which is heard') cited as one of the two foundational authorities for the rule of good conduct.
entities.justification: Śruti is explicitly invoked alongside Smṛti as the scriptural warrant for the conduct rules the text is prescribing.

mentions.quote: the rule of good conduct, which is the root of Dharma, as declared in *Śruti* and *Smṛti*
mentions.role: scriptural authority for the rule of good conduct

entities.description: The remembered/traditional corpus of law and custom cited alongside Śruti as the twin authorities authorising the conduct rules.
entities.justification: Smṛti is explicitly named as the second scriptural authority for the good-conduct rules prescribed in this window.

themes.topic: Good conduct (ācāra) as the root of Dharma and source of prosperity

mentions.quote: the rule of good conduct, which is the root of Dharma, as declared in *Śruti* and *Smṛti*
From good conduct one indeed obtains long life; from good conduct, desired progeny; from good conduct, imperishable wealth
a man of bad conduct is condemned in the world; he is a constant partaker of sorrow, is afflicted with disease, and is short-lived
Even a man devoid of all auspicious marks, if he is of good conduct, full of faith, and free from envy, lives for a hundred years

themes.justification: Multiple consecutive verses (Mn_4.155–4.158) define good conduct as the foundational religious and social virtue, treating it as causally productive of all worldly and spiritual goods.

themes.topic: Autonomy and self-reliance as the criterion of happiness

mentions.quote: Whatever action is dependent on others, that he should diligently avoid; but whatever is dependent on himself, that he should diligently perform
All that is dependent on others is suffering; all that is dependent on oneself is happiness
That action in the performance of which his inner soul finds satisfaction, that he should perform with diligence

themes.justification: Verses Mn_4.159–4.161 form a compact teaching that equates dependence with suffering and inner satisfaction with the guide for right action, presenting a philosophy of self-determination.

themes.topic: Non-violence toward Brahmanas and the karmic consequences of harming them

mentions.quote: A twice-born who, with the desire to kill, merely threatens a Brahmana, wanders for a hundred years in the hell called Tamisra
Having struck him in anger and intentionally, even with a blade of grass, he is born for twenty-one births in sinful wombs
A man who, through foolishness, causes blood to flow from the body of a Brahmana who is not fighting, obtains very great suffering after death
a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born, nor strike him even with a blade of grass, nor cause blood to flow from his body

themes.justification: A sequence of verses (Mn_4.165–4.169) elaborates graded punishments—hellish wandering, rebirth in sinful wombs, post-mortem torment—for progressively serious acts of violence against Brahmanas.

themes.topic: Karma, delayed retribution, and the gradual fruition of unrighteousness

mentions.quote: Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow; but turning slowly, it cuts the roots of the doer
If not upon himself, then upon his sons; if not upon his sons, then upon his grandsons; but an unrighteous act once done is never fruitless
Through unrighteousness one prospers for a time, then one sees good things, then one conquers one's enemies; but in the end, one perishes to the root

themes.justification: Verses Mn_4.172–4.174 develop a sustained theory of delayed but inevitable karmic retribution, using the cow and tree-root as analogies for slow but certain fruition.

themes.topic: Cosmological mapping of social roles onto divine worlds

mentions.quote: The *ācārya* is the lord of the world of Brahma; the father is the lord in the world of Prajapati; the guest is the lord of the world of Indra
The daughters-in-law are lords in the world of the Apsaras; the kinsmen, of the Vishve-devas; the relatives, of the world of the waters
The child, the old, the emaciated, and the sick are to be known as lords of the ether; an elder brother is equal to a father

themes.justification: Verses Mn_4.182–4.184 systematically assign every social role (teacher, father, guest, kin, wife, servants) a corresponding divine cosmic realm, encoding social ethics in a cosmological framework.

themes.topic: Dangers of accepting gifts for unlearned or unqualified Brahmanas

mentions.quote: by accepting gifts, his spiritual luster is quickly extinguished
A wise man, without knowing the righteous rule for accepting various things, should not accept a gift, even if he is perishing from hunger
An unlearned man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothes, sesame seeds, or ghee is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood
A twice-born who has not performed *tapas* and has not studied, but is fond of accepting gifts, sinks with that gift, like one crossing water on a raft of stone
an unlearned man should be afraid of accepting a gift from any source whatsoever; for even with a small gift, an unlearned man sinks like a cow in the mud

themes.justification: A cluster of verses (Mn_4.186–4.191) repeatedly warns that receiving gifts without the requisite learning and tapas destroys the recipient spiritually, treating gift-acceptance as a major ethical hazard for unqualified twice-born.

themes.topic: Avoidance of hypocrites who use Dharma as a cloak for vice (cat's vow / heron's mode)

mentions.quote: A knower of Dharma should not give even water to a twice-born who follows the cat's vow, nor to a sinful one who follows the heron's mode of life
He who makes a banner of his Dharma, is always greedy, deceitful, a hypocrite in the eyes of the world, violent, and a slanderer of all—he is to be known as one who follows the cat's vow

themes.justification: Verses Mn_4.192 and 4.195 frame religious hypocrisy—using Dharma as a public banner while being inwardly greedy and violent—as a distinct ethical category deserving complete social exclusion.

themes.topic: Ancestral path and following the conduct of one's forebears

mentions.quote: The path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the good he should go; by going that way, he is not harmed

themes.justification: Verse Mn_4.178 valorises adherence to ancestral precedent as a protective and ethically sufficient guide, grounding the conservative norm of tradition-following.

themes.topic: Avoidance of disputes with household members and the liberating effect of such restraint

mentions.quote: With a sacrificial priest, a family priest, an *ācārya*, a maternal uncle, a guest, a dependent, a child, an old man, a sick person, a physician, a kinsman, a relative, and a friend
With his mother and father, with his daughters-in-law, with his brother, son, and wife, with his daughter, and with his servants—he should not engage in a dispute
By abandoning disputes with these, he is freed from all sins; and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds

themes.justification: Verses Mn_4.179–4.181 enumerate an exhaustive list of persons with whom dispute is forbidden, promising liberation from sin and cosmic conquest as the reward for restraint.
